title: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal
hookLine: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal

cards: Next to the Golden Temple in Amritsar there's a kitchen that never closes. Anyone can walk in and eat: no ticket, no questions. People at the temple speak of tens of thousands of meals on an ordinary day.
And there are no chairs. A banker sits beside a laborer, a first-time visitor beside a grandmother who's come for sixty years, all on the floor in long rows. Where you sit usually says who you are.

teach.h: LANGAR — THE KITCHEN AND THE MEAL.
teach.b: Langar is the free community kitchen, and the meal that comes out of it. Gurdwaras keep one.
Tradition traces it to Guru Nanak, who shared food with everyone who came to his town of Kartarpur, and the Gurus after him built it into an institution. Here's why it mattered.
In Nanak's Punjab, caste rules decided who could eat with whom, and who could even cook for whom.

teach.h: EATING ACROSS THE LINES OF CASTE.
teach.b: Eating side by side across those lines could be a scandal. The langar did it on purpose, every day.
The row everyone sits in even has its own name: pangat. Three details carry the idea. The floor: nobody sits higher, because there's nothing to sit higher on.
The food: simple and vegetarian, so someone of any faith or diet can eat without asking what's in it.

teach.h: THE FLOOR, THE FOOD, THE GUEST LIST.
teach.b: And the guest list: there isn't one. Any faith, or none. You sit down, hold out your hands, and someone puts a roti in them.
The meal is a teaching you can taste: one God, one row.

how: Gurdwaras run a langar: volunteers cook a simple vegetarian meal and serve it free to anyone, traditionally seated together in rows on the floor.

games.why: the langar puts everyone on the floor in one row, the pangat, eating the same food. nobody sits higher.

practice: One breath with the bell. Picture yourself in the row: on your left, someone you'd never usually sit beside; on your right, someone else. Breathe in.
As you breathe out, hold out your hands, palms up, the way people do when the roti comes down the row.
